KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Strong high pressure and very dry air across northern New 
England will keep conditions dry through Friday. Moisture does begin 
to increase tonight and into Friday associated with the nor'easter 
approaching southern New England from the south, but this looks to 
be mainly in the form of mid and high clouds...so currently not 
expecting any precip during the day Friday. The high clouds may keep 
lows tonight a little milder than the previous couple, but temps 
across the north and interior could still get into the low-mid 30s 
to allow some frost development. Valley fog is also again likely 
across northern valleys and the CT River. Northeast winds will pick 
up Friday with gusts around 20-25 mph and maybe 25-35 mph closer to 
the seacoast.  

Friday will also see deteriorating marine and surf conditions that 
will remain dangerous and all the way through the weekend and 
possibly through Monday. Seas will continue to build from arriving 
swells and a long and continuous fetch of northeast winds. This will 
result in large breaking waves along the coast and a high risk of 
rip currents, and the High Surf Advisory remains unchanged. 

High astronomical tides will also be on the upward trend this 
weekend, and increasing surge to around 2' could push waters levels 
close to minor flood stage around the times of high tide. However, 
sometimes surge guidance can be underdone in long and persistent 
northeast flow. So future forecasts could be adjusted upward, 
and that would probably require a Coastal Flood Advisory for 
portions of the coast.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Regarding rainfall...As the low moves up the coast, it will be 
fighting dry high pressure to the north. Thus, it may take a while 
for the atmosphere to moisten and for precipitation to start 
falling. The ECMWF continues to trend further south which would 
delay rain onset to mainly Saturday while the GFS and Canadian 
deterministic solutions would suggest rain starting across our south 
Friday night. If high pressure remains strong, the ECMWF solution 
could still be on the table even if it is an outlier which may keep 
some of the heavier rainfall bands south. Further complicating the 
rainfall factor is that there could be a convective element with 
forecast soundings suggesting the potential for some instability at 
times with embedded downpours. All that said, the rainfall forecast 
remains one of the more uncertain factors regarding the nor'easter 
as it remains highly dependent on the eventual track. The best 
chances will be across southern New Hampshire and coastal/interior 
Maine where the NBM suggests a 50 to 80 percent chance for at least 
an inch of rain and 30 to 60 percent chance for at least two inches 
(48-hour totals). Over these locations, a widespread 1 to 2 inches 
seems to be a reasonable forecast with locally higher amounts up to 
4 inches possible. The one caveat is that we could see lower totals 
with a southern trend.

Regarding the winds...a tight pressure gradient will setup with 
anomalous high pressure to our north and anomalous low pressure to 
our south which will lead to gusty northeast winds. NAM and GFS 
soundings suggest that we will see winds in the 35 to 45 knot range 
at the top of the mixed layer, potentially starting late Friday 
night and lasting through the day on Sunday. Thus, we could end up 
seeing some Wind Advisory criteria gusts up to 45 mph at times along 
the coast and into the interior during this timeframe. 

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...

The upper low will stall and be slow to move out of the region,
keeping precipitation chances in the forecast on Monday and
possibly into Tuesday. Global models are starting to come into
better agreement that we could see another round of locally
heavy rainfall Sunday night into Monday as the upper low
meanders north northeast along the coast. We will need to watch
trends as models will likely struggle with resolving this low
predictability pattern. 

A progressive ridge will then cross the region sometime midweek
followed by a quick moving wave/frontal system. Temperatures may
also trend warmer by mid week with widespread lower 70s
returning to the forecast by Wednesday or Thursday.
